general_conventions: M1 = method mark; A marks dependent on it cannot be scored unless the M mark is earned. A1 = accuracy/answer mark, often awarded for a correct final answer which then implies earlier C marks.
C1 = compensatory (method) mark that can be awarded for correct working even if the final answer is wrong; a correct final answer normally earns all C marks.
B1 = independent mark, not dependent on other marks.
A0 on a show-that line means the given value earns no credit by itself; the mark is for the working shown.

ECF (error carried forward): later numerical parts can earn full credit if consistent with an earlier wrong answer; ECF is allowed after arithmetic (AE), transcription (TE) and power-of-ten (POT) errors but not after wrong physics/equation (XP).
POT: power-of-ten error, usually from SI prefix conversion; the mark where it happens is lost, then ECF applies.
TE: wrong copying of data from question, graph, booklet or earlier answer; lose that mark only, then ECF.
XP: using an incorrect equation counts as wrong physics even if it gives the right number.
SF: giving more significant figures than justified is not penalised; too few sig figs is handled within individual mark points and penalised only once in the paper.
CON: contradictory statements in one answer score no mark. BOD = benefit of the doubt.

Conventions: '/' separates alternative acceptable answers; Reject/Not = not creditworthy; Ignore = irrelevant; Allow = acceptable; words in brackets are not essential; underlined words must appear; AW = alternative wording; ORA = or reverse argument.

Level of Response (6-mark, asterisked) questions are marked holistically: decide the level from the science and the quality of reasoning, then the higher/lower mark within the level by communication. L1 = 1-2, L2 = 3-4, L3 = 5-6 marks; L1^/L2^/L3^ annotate the lower mark in each level.

LoR communication strands: L3 needs a well-developed line of reasoning, clear and logically structured, relevant and substantiated; L2 a line of reasoning with some structure, mostly relevant, supported by some evidence; L1 basic, unstructured information with limited evidence; 0 = nothing worthy of credit.
Alternative correct approaches and unexpected methods must be credited fairly.

questions.context: Meaning of coherent for two wave sources.
questions.answer: Constant phase difference between the waves
marking_points: B1: waves have a constant phase difference
pitfalls: Saying 'same frequency' or 'in phase' alone without constant phase difference

questions.context: Path difference at first minimum J from two given distances to the speakers.
Phase difference in radians at the first minimum.
Show wavelength is 0.16 m from path difference at the minimum.
marking_points: M1: path difference = λ/2 so λ = 2 × 0.08 (or use path difference at K = λ)
allow_reject_ignore: Allow use of path difference at K (0.16 m = λ)
pitfalls: Just restating 0.16 without linking to λ/2

questions.context: How an oscilloscope trace is used to find the frequency of sound.
questions.answer: Use timebase to get the period from the trace; f = 1/T
marking_points: B1: period determined using the timebase setting (divisions × time/div)
allow_reject_ignore: Allow one mark for f = 1/T if T not defined
pitfalls: Not mentioning the timebase / horizontal scale

questions.context: Speed of sound from frequency 2.1 kHz and wavelength.
allow_reject_ignore: Allow 1 mark for 0.336 or 0.34 (POT from kHz)

questions.context: Physical quantity given by area under loading curve.
marking_points: B1: energy (elastic potential energy) / work done on the rubber
allow_reject_ignore: Allow work done on the band

questions.context: Energy transferred stretching rubber to 0.25 m from curved graph.
marking_points: C1: value of one square identified (e.g. 1 cm^2 = 0.025 m × 2.5 N = 0.0625 J) or other valid area method
allow_reject_ignore: Do not accept 0.5Fx (graph is not linear)
pitfalls: Using ½Fx for a non-linear curve

questions.context: Why energy returned on unloading differs from energy input.
questions.answer: Some energy transferred as heat (internal energy) to the rubber/surroundings
marking_points: B1: energy dissipated as heat to the rubber/surroundings

questions.context: Effect on stored energy when diameter doubled, same load and material.

A1: elastic energy decreases by factor of 4

questions.subtopic: elastic and inelastic collisions on an air track
questions.context: Use calculations to explain two glider collisions using momentum, elastic and inelastic.
questions.answer: Momentum conserved in both (0.15 kg m s^-1); Expt 1 elastic (KE 0.015 J conserved), Expt 2 inelastic (KE falls to 0.0056 J)
marking_points: L3 (5-6): clear explanation of terms and of results, correctly comparing momentum and kinetic energy for both experiments; well-developed logical reasoning
L2 (3-4): clear explanation of terms with limited explanation of results comparing momentum, OR limited terms with some results, OR correct comparison of momentum and KE
L1 (1-2): limited explanation of terms or limited comparison of momentum/KE
Indicative: p = mv; Ek = ½mv²; total momentum and total energy always conserved; KE conserved only in elastic collision; in elastic collision relative speed of approach = speed of separation
Indicative: initial momentum of A = 0.15 kg m s^-1, initial KE = 0.015 J
Indicative Expt 1: separation speed 0.200 m s^-1; p_A after = -0.0375, p_B = 0.1875, total 0.15 kg m s^-1; KE after 0.00094 + 0.01406 = 0.015 J, so elastic
Indicative Expt 2: p after = 0.15 kg m s^-1; KE after 0.0056 J, so inelastic; momentum conserved in both
pitfalls: Forgetting the rebound velocity is negative
Saying total energy is lost in inelastic collisions rather than KE
Not doing the calculations the question requires

questions.subtopic: impulse as area under F-t graph
questions.context: Speed of golf ball from triangular force-time graph and its mass.
marking_points: C1: impulse = area = ½ × 0.4 × 18 = 3.6 N s

questions.context: Show cross-sectional area of cylinder ≈ 6.6 × 10^-4 m².
pitfalls: Not showing the value to more s.f. than given

questions.context: Weight of wooden cylinder from area, height and density.
Depth of floating cylinder below water surface.
marking_points: C1: mass (or volume) of water displaced = weight / g: 0.0316 kg or volume 3.16 × 10^-5 m³
C1: y = volume displaced / cross-sectional area
pitfalls: Not realising upthrust = weight for floating object

questions.context: New depth when floating in oil of density 900 kg m^-3, with explanation.
questions.answer: 0.053 m; deeper because same weight of less dense fluid needs bigger volume
marking_points: B1: same weight/mass of oil displaced
B1: lower density means larger volume of oil displaced
pitfalls: Saying upthrust is smaller in oil (it is the same, equal to weight)

questions.context: Use Kirchhoff's second law to derive terminal p.d. equation.
questions.answer: E = V + Ir so V = E - Ir
marking_points: C1: sum of e.m.f.s = sum of p.d.s (E = V + Ir)
A1: rearranged to V = E - Ir
pitfalls: Not stating the law in terms of e.m.f. and p.d. around a loop

questions.context: How E and r are obtained from V against I graph.
allow_reject_ignore: E and r must be the subject

questions.context: Resistance of variable resistor at 25 mA using V from graph.
Energy dissipated in resistor in 5.0 minutes.
Charge through resistor in 5.0 minutes with unit.
Design LDR potential divider giving >5 V in bright light, <1 V in dark, with values and adjustment.
questions.answer: Supply ≥6 V; voltmeter across fixed resistor in series with LDR; fixed R chosen e.g. ~kΩ-tens of kΩ; variable resistor to adjust threshold
marking_points: L3 (5-6): correct circuit diagram and explanation including detailed calculations and explanation of adjustment for different light intensities; clear logical reasoning
L2 (3-4): a diagram with some calculations/explanation
L1 (1-2): limited diagram with voltmeter wrongly placed and limited calculations, OR correct diagram with correct symbols
Indicative (diagram): potential divider; correct symbols; supply of at least 6.0 V; voltmeter across the fixed resistor
Indicative (calculations): potential divider equation; suitable fixed/variable resistor value; Vout calculated for very bright and for dark conditions
Indicative (adjustment): use a variable resistor; effect of increasing/decreasing its resistance on Vout
pitfalls: Placing output across the LDR (gives opposite behaviour)
Supply below 6 V cannot give >5 V
No numerical check of both conditions

questions.context: Show gradient of V against 1/λ line ≈ 1.2 × 10^-6 V m.
marking_points: B1: points read from line to nearest half square
B1: triangle bigger than half the line, Δy/Δx with correct power of ten shown

questions.context: Find h from gradient = hc/e, to 2 s.f.
Draw worst acceptable straight line through error bars.
questions.answer: Steepest or shallowest line passing through all error bars
marking_points: B1: steepest or shallowest line through all error bars
allow_reject_ignore: Note guidance on which error bar the steepest line must pass through

questions.context: Percentage uncertainty in h using worst-line gradient.
marking_points: M1: worst gradient determined, e.g. 1.0 or 1.4 × 10^-6 V m
pitfalls: Using difference in h computed with wrong scaling

questions.context: Maximum KE (J) of photoelectrons from aluminium (φ = 4.1 eV) with 98 nm radiation.
allow_reject_ignore: Allow 1.3 × 10^-18 J if 6.4 × 10^-34 used for h

questions.context: Effect on KEmax of reducing intensity at fixed wavelength.
questions.answer: No change; intensity only changes photon rate, photon energy depends on f
marking_points: M1: KE independent of intensity / intensity only affects number of photons (photon energy depends only on frequency)
allow_reject_ignore: Allow: lower intensity means fewer photons per second
pitfalls: Saying fewer electrons have less energy
